title: AI was supposed to hit new grads hard. So far, unemployment data says otherwise.
gist: A CESifo working paper using Census CPS microdata finds summer 2026 unemployment among recent US college graduates (7.3%) was within its 2022-2025 range and shows no statistically significant AI-driven displacement, contradicting a Stanford/ADP study and warnings from Marc Andreessen and Larry Fink, though the authors caution the classes of 2027+ may be more affected.

themes.theme: No AI hit to new grads yet

insights.claim: A CESifo working paper by Robert Fairlie and Jane Wu finds no evidence of significant, widespread displacement or reduced hiring of recent US college graduates due to AI, in absolute or relative terms.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Cuts against the popular 'AI is killing entry-level jobs' narrative; labor-market data do not yet show AI productivity substituting for junior workers at scale.
insights.quote: there is no evidence of any significant, widespread displacement or reduction in hiring of recent college graduates in absolute or relative levels

insights.claim: Summer 2026 unemployment for US bachelor's graduates aged 22-25 was 7.3 percent, within the prior range of 6.3 percent (2022) to 7.8 percent (2024).
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Young-graduate unemployment is not flashing a recession or AI-shock signal.

insights.claim: Comparing recent grads with non-college peers, older graduates aged 30-49, and by AI-exposure of occupations, the 2022-2026 trend differences were almost all statistically insignificant.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Even high-AI-exposure occupations show no distinct employment deterioration yet.

insights.claim: The Stanford study showing weaker entry-level employment in AI-impacted occupations used ADP payroll data measuring job supply, while the CESifo unemployment measure also reflects aggregate demand, which can shift even as AI contracts jobs in specific fields.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Occupation-level job losses can coexist with stable aggregate unemployment; watch both payroll-by-occupation and CPS data.

insights.claim: The mechanism researchers watch is firms cutting new hiring for standardized entry-level tasks rather than laying off experienced staff, so AI effects would appear first among recent graduates.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Graduate hiring is the leading indicator for AI labor substitution.

insights.claim: A Census survey shows a recent sharp increase in firms replacing many employee tasks with AI, alongside broad increases in AI spending per employee and ChatGPT Enterprise token use over the past 12 months.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI adoption and spend is accelerating, a demand signal for AI vendors even before labor effects show.

insights.claim: Marc Andreessen said AI was not good enough to do the jobs being cut until December 2025, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned in March 2026 that this year's graduates could see their highest unemployment in years even without a recession.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: High-profile predictions of AI-driven graduate unemployment have so far not materialized in the data.

insights.claim: The CESifo researchers warn that if workplace AI intensity keeps rising, the graduating classes of 2027 and later may be more affected than the class of 2026.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Keep monitoring summer 2027 graduate unemployment as the next test of AI labor displacement.
